power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Infant visual attention-most often operationalized through looking behavior-is a foundational method and explanatory construct in the study of early cognition.

Cultural psychology has established that attention is organized by culturally structured practices and localized meanings, but this work has focused largely on children and adults, and the extent to which culturally patterned experience shapes the endogenous attentional processes that looking measures are used to index in infancy remains under-specified.

This review focuses on the first two years of life and on four components of endogenous attention that are routinely inferred from looking behavior: focal versus contextual allocation, orienting speed versus accuracy, novelty versus familiarity orientation, and persistence versus flexibility.

We distinguish cultureshared meanings, practices, and organized forms of everyday activity-from demographic indicators such as nationality, language background, race, and socioeconomic status, which are coarse proxies for proximal experience.

Synthesizing cross-national studies alongside research on multilingual, interracial, and socioeconomic experience, we show that components of infant attention vary with experience and task context in ways that do not map cleanly onto reified group categories.

We identify a gap between research documenting effects of specific experiences and research examining culture directly, and we propose a culturally situated model in which endogenous attentional mechanisms are calibrated through culturally patterned input across development.
This approach preserves the value of looking-time and eye-tracking methods while strengthening their construct validity, measurement invariance, and generalizability.
Public significance statement: Infants' looking behavior is widely used to understand early learning, memory, and perception.
This paper shows that visual attention is also shaped by culturally patterned experiences, including language exposure, social diversity, and socioeconomic context.

Recognizing these influences can help developmental scientists interpret infants' behavior more accurately, avoid treating differences as deficits, and build theories and methods that better represent children growing up in diverse environments.

Infant attention-most often operationalized through looking behavior-is a central explanatory construct for a wide range of early mental processes, from perception and learning to memory, expectation formation, and emerging social cognition (Aslin, 2007; Colombo, 2001; Fantz, 1956; Oakes, 2023).

text.text: Over the last 50 years, infant looking time has emerged as the methodological backbone of infant psychological development.
A longstanding reliance on infant visual attention has often rested on a particular interpretive assumption.

This assumption is not that experience is irrelevant, but that looking behavior can be treated as sufficiently comparable across infants and samples to support broad developmental inferences unless a specific experiential factor is under investigation.
The assumption is especially consequential when looking measures are used to characterize developmental change, compare populations, or extrapolate from restricted samples to infants universally.

Indeed, infant research has often presumed that early behavioral responses provide insight into species-typical or universal psychological processes because infants are viewed as having relatively little prior experience (Singh, 2026, in press).

text.text: This experience is also culturally organized from the outset: infants encounter variation in linguistic input, caregiving routines, nutrition, and social and physical affordances that is structured by family life, institutions, and broader cultural practices, and such patterned conditions shape development even before birth (Singh, in press).
text.formatted: This experience is also culturally organized from the outset: infants encounter variation in linguistic input, caregiving routines, nutrition, and social and physical affordances that is structured by family life, institutions, and broader cultural practices, and such patterned conditions shape development even before birth <ref type="bibr">(Singh, in press)</ref>.

text.text: Infants are therefore never truly "acultural," and the visual attention they display may reflect culturally situated experience rather than an experience-independent starting point.
We do not claim that prior work has ignored experience-dependent attention.
Rather, we identify an interpretive default in which contextual influences remain peripheral unless they are explicitly measured or theorized.

Assessing the validity of this assumption is further complicated by evidence from meta-analyses showing that even basic demographic and contextual information-including where a study was conducted-is often incompletely reported in infant research (Singh, Cristia, et al., 2023; Singh & Rajendra, 2024).

text.text: Such omissions make it difficult to situate looking measures within infants' developmental contexts, evaluate assumptions of comparability and universality, and determine how sampling characteristics may shape the interpretation and generalizability of findings.

Foundational work has long shown that perceptual experience, stimulus familiarity, maturation, and task demands shape infant looking behavior (e.g., Colombo, 2001; Fantz, 1964; Johnson, 1990; Kidd & Hayden, 2015).

text.text: Cultural psychology has, in parallel, established that attention is organized by culturally structured practices and meanings.

In adults, East Asian participants attend more to context and to relations among elements, whereas North American participants attend more to focal objects (Chua et al., 2005; Kitayama et al., 2003; Masuda & Nisbett, 2001; Nisbett et al., 2001).

text.text: The claim that culturally patterned environments shape attentional development is therefore not new.
The present review makes three contributions that this literature leaves open.
First, it focuses on infancy.
Most cross-cultural research on attention has studied children from the preschool years onward, as well as adults, often using verbal, categorization, or free-viewing tasks.

Whether culturally patterned differences in attention are already present in the first two years before children produce the descriptions and narratives that reveal cultural modes of attention later in development (Senzaki et al., 2014 (Senzaki et al., , 2016) ) has only recently become an empirical question (e.g., Heise et al., 2025; Köster et al., 2023; Tu et al., 2025; Waxman et al., 2016).

text.text: Second, it focuses on endogenous attention processes, and specifically on the the components of attentional control that looking-time paradigms are designed to index, rather than on broad cognitive styles.
Third, it focuses on measurement.

Because looking behavior is the primary dependent variable from which infant learning, memory, and expectation are inferred, culturally patterned variation in its components has direct consequences for how infant findings are interpreted, compared, and generalized.
What remains less developed, and what we aim to provide, is a component-level account of how sociocultural experience interacts with endogenous attentional systems to shape these dependent measures.

We use endogenous attention to refer to the internally guided control of attention-selecting, sustaining, and shifting attention on the basis of the infant's expectations, goals, and prior learning-as distinct from exogenous attention, in which attention is captured by factors such as the physical salience of stimuli (Colombo, 2001; Colombo & Cheatham, 2006).

text.text: Across the first year, attention shifts from predominantly exogenous, stimulus-driven orienting toward increasing endogenous control, supported by the maturation of cortical attention networks (Johnson, 1990; Posner & Rothbart, 2007).

text.text: Endogenous attention is therefore the level at which accumulated experience would be expected have an impact.

We concentrate on four endogenous components that are routinely measured with looking-time and eyetracking paradigms: (a) the allocation of attention between focal objects and their context; (b) the control of orienting and disengagement; (c) novelty versus familiarity orientation; and (d) persistence versus flexibility in sustaining or redistributing attention.
Studies are reviewed when they inform one or more of these components.
Our scope is intentionally circumscribed.

We focus on these four components in infants from birth to approximately 24 months, rather than on every cognitive process inferred from looking time or on specialized social-attention processes such as gaze following.

We also do not claim that all looking or eye-tracking measures are equally susceptible to sociocultural variation; some measures appear robust across markedly different contexts (Gredebäck et al., 2025).

text.text: Nor do the concerns we raise apply only to cross-group comparisons.

Studies of a single cultural group are also conducted within a particular cultural ecology, and the same interpretive questions arise whenever findings from that group are generalized to infants more broadly or treated as evidence of universal processes (Nielsen et al., 2017; Singh, 2026).
text.formatted: Studies of a single cultural group are also conducted within a particular cultural ecology, and the same interpretive questions arise whenever findings from that group are generalized to infants more broadly or treated as evidence of universal processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Nielsen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Singh, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Within-participant designs can control for stable experiential differences among infants in a sample, which can make cultural dependency less consequential for these designs, but they do not establish that the task engages the same construct, or yields effects of the same magnitude, in infants raised under different conditions.

Cultural dependency becomes most critical when researchers compare groups, pool samples, interpret baseline looking differences, test generalizability, or assume that a task engages the same construct across sociocultural contexts.
And without basic demographic data, it is difficult to evaluate any of these possibilities.
We do not argue that infant attention is primarily exogenous or that culturally patterned experience replaces endogenous theories of attentional development.
Rather, we adopt an interactionist position.

Contemporary accounts already conceptualize alerting, orienting, and executive attention as biologically constrained systems that develop through continuous interaction with experience (e.g., Colombo & Cheatham, 2006; Posner & Rothbart, 2007).
text.formatted: Contemporary accounts already conceptualize alerting, orienting, and executive attention as biologically constrained systems that develop through continuous interaction with experience (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Colombo & Cheatham, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Posner & Rothbart, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Our central question is therefore not whether attention is endogenous or experience-dependent, but how endogenous attentional systems become calibrated through culturally patterned environments across development and how these interactions can form a part of theory.

Across the literatures reviewed below, we use the four components defined above to interpret sociocultural variation in attentional allocation: (a) focal versus contextual processing, (b) speed versus accuracy, (c) novelty versus familiarity orientation, and (d) persistence versus flexibility.
We first review cross-national studies, which most directly address culture but measure it coarsely.
We then review, more briefly, research on multilingual, interracial, and socioeconomic experience.
These literatures do not study culture as such.

They are included because each isolates a dimension of proximal experience-variability of linguistic input, social diversity, and environmental predictability-that is often bundled with culture in cross-national comparisons.

Our coverage is also necessarily constrained by how the primary studies have operationalized culture: almost exclusively through demographic proxies such as country of residence, language background, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status, rather than through direct measures of the shared values, beliefs, socialization goals, caregiving practices, and everyday routines that constitute culture.

We then consider the gap between these two bodies of work, synthesize the findings at the level of attentional components, and propose a culturally situated model of infant visual attention with practical implications for both large collaborative studies and typical single-laboratory designs.
Culture has been conceptualized in several ways, and the choice of definition shapes what counts as evidence of cultural influence.
Symbolic and interpretive approaches define culture as shared systems of meaning through which people interpret experience (Bruner, 1990; Geertz, 1973).

text.text: For infancy specifically, the developmental niche framework identifies three subsystems through which culture reaches the developing child: the physical and social settings of daily life, culturally regulated customs of childcare, and the psychology of caregivers (Super & Harkness, 1986; see also Keller, 2007).

text.text: Building on these perspectives, we use culture to refer to shared meanings, practices, values, interactional routines, and organized forms of everyday experience.
Nationality, language background, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status are not equivalent to culture.

They are best understood as coarse indicators that covary with culturally organized experience, such as caregiving routines, linguistic variability, social density, and environmental predictability, but also with factors that are not cultural in this sense, such as material resources and health.
The developmental niche framework is particularly relevant here because each of its subsystems can be translated into measurable proximal variables.

An important empirical charge is to move from broad indicators toward more precise measures of the proximal experiences that plausibly tune attention, and to be explicit about whether a given study examines culture or a correlate of it.
Cross-national comparisons provide one window onto early attentional variation, but they should not be interpreted as direct tests of culture by themselves.
National context is a broad proxy that can covary with caregiver practices, stimulus familiarity, urbanicity, language input, testing context, and analytic decisions.
Cross-national designs also face well-documented methodological limitations.

They confound culture with many co-occurring differences, often treat variation within countries as error variance, typically sample only two populations so that any difference has many possible sources, and can mistake differences in how a measure functions in context for differences in the construct it is meant to index (Matsumoto & Yoo, 2006; van de Vijver & Leung, 1997; see also Henrich et al., 2010; Nielsen et al., 2017).

text.text: We therefore use cross-national studies not to argue that nations impose fixed attentional styles, but to illustrate how culturally patterned environments may be associated with separable components of attention.
Historically, much of this work draws on the distinction between analytic and holistic cognition.

In Nisbett and colleagues' account, analytic thought involves detaching objects from their context, attending to their attributes, and reasoning about them with rules, whereas holistic thought involves attending to the field as a whole and to relations among its elements (Nisbett et al., 2001).

text.text: Object-versus background-oriented attention is a narrower construct.

It refers to the relative allocation of attention to focal objects versus their surrounding context, typically measured as fixation time to foreground versus background regions (Chua et al., 2005; Masuda & Nisbett, 2001).

text.text: The two are related but not equivalent: holistic processing also concerns how objects are integrated with their context and with one another, which allocation measures do not capture directly.

A higher proportion of looking to the background could therefore reflect contextual integration, but it could also reflect weaker engagement with the focal object or broader scanning without integration (see Tu et al., 2025).

For example, Hagihara et al. (2026) found that Japanese-and English-speaking 2-to 5-year-olds largely interpreted heard action verbs in terms of similarly narrow action categories, regardless of how broadly or narrowly each language's verbs apply.

Notably, some cultural differences in older participants emerge only when a task requires verbal description or narrative, and not during passive viewing (Senzaki et al., 2014 (Senzaki et al., , 2016)).

text.text: This raises the question of whether differences in attentional allocation can be observed in infancy, when looking-based measures are the primary window onto attention.

Recent cross-national eye-tracking work has investigated variation in foreground versus background processing, particularly in comparisons involving Eastern and Western contexts. Heise et al. (2025), for example, found that 15-month-olds in Japan devoted relatively more attention to background information than infants in the United States when viewing both faces and cartoon scenes, with the difference in the cartoon task most pronounced for background objects with eyes.

text.text: Swedish infants scanned more broadly, looked relatively longer at focal objects than at background information, and shifted gaze between focal elements and background more frequently than Zimbabwean infants.
They therefore combined an analytic emphasis on focal objects with broad exploration and frequent shifting, features typically associated with holistic viewing.
Zimbabwean infants made fewer fixations and looked less overall, and devoted relatively less attention to focal objects.
Within the Zimbabwean sample, greater poverty and stronger caregiver relatedness were associated with more distributed, holistic-looking patterns.

Relative to US infants, however, Malawian infants took longer to fixate the targets but were more accurate overall.
This pattern indicate a different trade-off between speed and accuracy across contexts.

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that the fundamental mechanisms of infant orienting are present across contexts, while their speed and accuracy may be shaped by infants' lived experiences, by the demands of the particular task, and by their interaction.
At the outset, we note that language background is not a proxy for culture; many bilingual infants share cultural practices with monolingual peers in the same community.

We include this literature because language exposure varies within cultural groups and isolates one proximal dimension of experience-the variability of linguistic input-that cross-national comparisons sometimes bundle with culture.
Lookingtime measures are widely used to infer infants' underlying knowledge and learning, yet the same magnitude or pattern of looking can arise from different attentional processes.

Classic accounts emphasize that infants' visual preferences shift from familiarity to novelty as a function of encoding, developmental stage, and task difficulty (Hunter & Ames, 1988; Roder et al., 2000; see also Kosie, Zettersten et al., 2024).

text.text: Within that tradition, novelty preferences are often used to infer memory or discrimination.

The point of the studies reviewed here is not that novelty preferences cease to be informative about memory, but that the timing, threshold, and strength of novelty orientation may themselves be shaped by infants' prior experience, including exposure to multiple languages.
Evidence from visual habituation and paired-comparison paradigms shows that bilingual exposure is associated with differences in both the rate and direction of attentional change.

In a study of Singaporean 6-month-olds, monolingual and bilingual infants showed comparable total fixation during visual habituation, but bilingual infants exhibited steeper habituation slopes and a reliable novelty preference at test when discriminating similar visual stimuli (Singh et al., 2015).

text.text: This pattern is consistent with rapid encoding alongside a stronger orientation toward novel information in bilingually exposed infants.

Because many infant studies interpret longer looking to novelty as evidence of discrimination, surprise, or memory, these findings indicate that experience can influence how readily such responses are expressed, even when the measure remains theoretically meaningful.
Language experience also modifies the temporal dynamics of attention.

Using gap-overlap and switching tasks, D 'Souza et al. (2020) showed that bilingually exposed infants disengaged from central stimuli more quickly and shifted attention to peripheral or changing stimuli sooner than monolingual peers.

text.text: Within bilingual infants, disengagement speed was associated with the amount of second-language exposure, and faster disengagement was associated with more frequent attentional switching.

These results indicate that bilingual infants sample visual information more broadly, consistent with adaptation to environments in which input is more variable and less predictable (see D 'Souza & D'Souza, 2021; Singh, 2021; Singh, Barr et al. 2024).

text.text: Similar effects emerge in visual preference paradigms designed to assess novelty orientation.

In a side-by-side task in which one stimulus remained constant while the other changed across trials, bilingually exposed infants showed earlier and more persistent preferences for the changing stimulus than monolingual infants, whose novelty preference emerged more gradually over time (Singh, Kalashnikova, & Quinn, 2023).
text.formatted: In a side-by-side task in which one stimulus remained constant while the other changed across trials, bilingually exposed infants showed earlier and more persistent preferences for the changing stimulus than monolingual infants, whose novelty preference emerged more gradually over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Singh, Kalashnikova, & Quinn, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the strength and timing of novelty preferences were related to degree of secondlanguage exposure, indicating a graded effect of language experience on attentional allocation.

These findings are particularly relevant for studies that use novelty preference as an index of learning, as they show that baseline preferences for novelty can differ systematically across infants before any experimental manipulation is introduced.
Anticipatory-looking paradigms further illustrate how language experience can influence the interpretation of gaze behavior.

Although early reports suggested bilingual advantages in anticipatory control (Kovács & Mehler, 2009), subsequent work has shown that group differences may lie less in anticipatory accuracy than in how rapidly infants orient once a salient outcome appears.

text.text: In a replication attempt, Kalashnikova et al. (2021) found no bilingual advantage in anticipatory looks but observed that bilingual infants fixated a novel visual reward preferentially relative to monolingual infants.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with enhanced responsiveness to novel stimuli rather than advantages in executive control.
Downstream consequences may extend to learning and generalization.

In deferred imitation tasks, bilingual infants generalize learned actions across greater changes in visual features than monolingual infants (Barr et al., 2020; Brito & Barr, 2012 , 2014), although these tasks index memory flexibility rather than attention per se.

text.text: Taken together, these findings indicate that language experience may tune attentional systems that underlie commonly used behavioral measures of nonlinguistic (i.e., visual) attention, and that measuring linguistic variation can clarify multiple dimensions of visual attention (Singh, Barokova et al., 2024).

text.text: The literature on interracial face experience is included to clarify the boundary between domainspecific and domain-general effects of experience on attention.

Face perception is often treated as a specialized domain, and the other-race effect has classically been interpreted in terms of perceptual narrowing and face-processing experience; it should not be collapsed uncritically with object-based looking paradigms.
It is relevant here insofar as it informs whether sociocultural experience influences the endogenous operations through which visual information is selected, maintained, and disengaged.

Across multiple studies, infants raised in relatively homogeneous racial environments tend to show early attentional biases toward, and selective discrimination of, own-race faces (Kelly et al., 2005; 2007; 2009).
text.formatted: Across multiple studies, infants raised in relatively homogeneous racial environments tend to show early attentional biases toward, and selective discrimination of, own-race faces <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Kelly et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">2009)</ref>.

text.text: Increased interracial exposure can attenuate or alter these biases. Bar-Haim et al. (2006) reported that 3-month-olds' own-race visual preference was modulated by exposure to other-race individuals, and Gaither et al. (2012) showed that monoracial and biracial infants differed in face processing and scanning patterns.

text.text: In a multiracial context, Singh, Phneah et al. (2022) found that both societal-level diversity and caregiving experience were associated with infants' race-related looking preferences.

text.text: Recent work also points to attentional mechanisms within the face domain itself.

Markant, Oakes, and Amso (2016) used a spatial cueing task to experimentally bias Caucasian 9-month-old infants' attention toward own-or other-race faces and found that infants discriminated the faces that were the focus of attention, regardless of race.
This suggests that differences in attentional engagement, rather than a loss of sensitivity to other-race faces, may be one mechanism through which experience shapes face discrimination.
A more speculative question is whether such attentional dynamics attributed to experience with social (racial) categories generalizes beyond faces.
D 'Souza, Rajendra, and Singh (submitted) examined infants' interracial contact as a predictor of performance on a gap-overlap attentional disengagement task using non-face stimuli.
text.formatted: D <ref type="bibr">'Souza, Rajendra, and Singh (submitted)</ref> examined infants' interracial contact as a predictor of performance on a gap-overlap attentional disengagement task using non-face stimuli.

text.text: In 9-to 11-month-old bilingual infants, greater interracial contact predicted more efficient attentional disengagement when shifting gaze from a central object to a competing peripheral object.
Two interpretations remain possible.

On a domain-specific account, interracial experience recalibrates attention within the social domain, altering how infants allocate attention to faces and social categories while leaving broader object-directed attention largely intact.
On a domain-general account, frequent exposure to socially and perceptually variable faces may also support more flexible orienting or disengagement across visual contexts.
Distinguishing between these possibilities will require studies that jointly measure infants' social exposure, attentional dynamics, and learning across both social and non-social tasks.

This distinction is important for the present framework because a culturally situated model should specify the scope of an experiential effect rather than assume that all experience-dependent changes generalize across domains.

Socioeconomic status (SES) has become a central construct in research on early attention because it indexes access to material resources and introduces associated systematic variation in infants' everyday experiences, including environmental predictability, caregiver interaction patterns, and exposure to cognitive stimulation (Duncan et al. 1994).
text.formatted: Socioeconomic status (SES) has become a central construct in research on early attention because it indexes access to material resources and introduces associated systematic variation in infants' everyday experiences, including environmental predictability, caregiver interaction patterns, and exposure to cognitive stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Duncan et al. 1994)</ref>.

text.text: A central construct in this section is environmental entropy, by which we mean the degree of unpredictability, variability, and informational disorder in infants' everyday environments.
Entropy may include household noise, crowding, interruption, visual clutter, caregiver availability, and instability in routines.
It is not synonymous with SES, although the two may covary.
Treating entropy as a proximal feature of experience helps distinguish material resources from the structure of attentional demands in the infant's environment.
Early evidence for SES differences in fixation comes from longitudinal work examining infant attention during free-play contexts.

Clearfield and Jedd (2013) followed infants from higher-and lower-SES households (classified by maternal education) longitudinally at 6, 9, and 12 months during free play with either a single toy or an array of six toys.
Higher-SES infants showed more focused attention to toys overall and greater increases in focused attention in the more complex six-toy condition.

Lower-SES infants showed more off-task looking at every age and in both conditions, and were less likely to modulate their attention according to stimulus complexity, most clearly at 12 months and in measures of disengagement and attention to people.

Clearfield and Jedd interpreted these patterns as early attention deficits, speculating about nutritional mechanisms and calling for early intervention, consistent with much of the historical framing of SES effects.
Studies of disengagement and orienting provide a more mechanistic view of fixation dynamics.

Studies using gap-overlap paradigms indicate that SES relates to how infants balance maintaining fixation against shifting attention, but these relations are not uniform across studies, samples, or ages.

For example, Siqueiros Sanchez et al. (2021) found that among 5-month-old Swedish infants, those whose mothers had more education showed slower gaze-shift latencies in the overlap condition (and in the baseline condition), although SES was unrelated to the disengagement difference score.

(2021)</ref> found that among 5-month-old Swedish infants, those whose mothers had more education showed slower gaze-shift latencies in the overlap condition (and in the baseline condition), although SES was unrelated to the disengagement difference score.

text.text: The authors suggested, with caution, that slower latencies may not indicate poorer performance in infancy, given that faster gaze shifts may come at a cost of accuracy, but they did not measure accuracy directly and noted that the effect was small.
These findings contrast with studies using other paradigms that report attentional disadvantages for lower-SES infants (e.g., Clearfield & Niman, 2012; Lipina et al., 2005).

text.text: An important interpretive question raised by these findings concerns the functional significance of attentional regulation in context.
Differences in sustained engagement or modulation with complexity need not reflect deficits in attentional capacity; they may instead reflect calibration to environmental demands.

For example, if lower-SES environments are more perceptually cluttered, less predictable, or characterized by higher levels of background activity and interruption, broader sampling or heightened vigilance may be advantageous for monitoring multiple information sources rather than sustaining prolonged focus on a single object.

From this perspective, modulation of fixation across experimental conditions could reflect an attentional pattern tuned to contexts in which sustained focus is not consistently rewarded, motivating mechanistic work that targets the engagement-disengagement equilibrium and its expression relative to contextual demands.
Longitudinal evidence further highlights the need to distinguish between disengagement speed and disengagement failure.

For example, Moyano et al. (2023) found no significant associations between a composite SES index measured at 6 months and visual disengagement at any age, although SES showed a trend toward fewer disengagement failures at 16-18 months.

text.text: When individual SES components were examined, higher parental occupational status at 6 months was associated with fewer failures to disengage at 16-18 months, whereas parental education and income-to-needs were not.
In hierarchical regression models, the SES index at 6 months predicted fewer disengagement failures at 16-18 months even after accounting for disengagement performance at 9 months.

The authors interpreted these findings as consistent with prior work linking higher SES to more focused attention and greater attentional flexibility in infancy (Clearfield & Jedd, 2013; Clearfield & Niman, 2012; Lipina et al., 2005) and with later SES-related differences in attentional control (Hackman & Farah, 2009).

text.text: Infants' home environments also vary in ways that SES does not fully capture, particularly household disorganization and chaos, which may exert independent and sometimes counterintuitive effects on attention.

In Moyano et al. (2023), SES and chaos made independent contributions to later disengagement, and, contrary to the authors' hypothesis, higher levels of chaos at 6 months predicted fewer disengagement failures at 16-18 months.

text.text: The authors proposed that unpredictable home environments may foster a more reactive attentional style and heightened sensitivity to contextual information, which could facilitate disengagement from a central stimulus but might undermine attentional control in situations that require ignoring competing information.

Consistent with this account, a related study found that 2-to 4year-olds from more disorganized homes made more correct anticipations in complex, context-dependent visual sequences (Moyano et al., 2022).

text.text: By contrast, Tomalski et al. (2017) found that among 5.5-montholds from predominantly middle-class families, greater parent-reported household chaos was associated with longer looking, and thus slower processing, of complex but not simple stimuli in a habituation task.

(2017)</ref> found that among 5.5-montholds from predominantly middle-class families, greater parent-reported household chaos was associated with longer looking, and thus slower processing, of complex but not simple stimuli in a habituation task.

text.text: Family income did not predict looking in this model, although it did when household size was used as an indirect measure of crowding.
The authors interpreted chaos as detrimental to processing speed under high task demands.

In trying to reconcile these findings, associations between household chaos and infant visual attention are not uniformly directional; instead, they appear vary by which attentional component is measured and the structure of the task.

In habituation paradigms indexing processing efficiency, higher chaos predicts slower processing under high stimulus demands (e.g., longer peak looks to complex scenes; Tomalski et al., 2017) that could reflect attentional overwhelm, whereas in gap-overlap paradigms indexing disengagement, higher chaos predicts fewer failures to disengage by toddlerhood (Moyano et al., 2023), a pattern that may reflect a more reactive, vigilance-oriented attentional style rather than enhanced sustained processing.

text.text: More work is needed to clarify when attentional patterns function as context-sensitive adaptations that support learning, versus when they may carry downstream processing costs in settings that reward sustained attention.

One example of such a component-based approach comes from studies of object-and feature-based attention. Werchan et al. (2019) examined how 3-to 5-and 9-to 12-month-olds resolve competition between whole-object representations and salient perceptual features (color, orientation, and motion), and explored whether family income related to this process.

(2019)</ref> examined how 3-to 5-and 9-to 12-month-olds resolve competition between whole-object representations and salient perceptual features (color, orientation, and motion), and explored whether family income related to this process.

text.text: Higher income was associated with greater featurebased attention among younger infants and, as a trend, with greater object-based attention among older infants, but only when color competed with object identity; income was unrelated to performance on orientation or motion trials.
These feature-specific effects may reflect interactions between SES-related experience and the developmental status of particular visual processing pathways.
From this perspective, SES does not globally enhance attention but may shape attentional selection as representational systems mature.

The authors proposed that income may influence the number and variability of infants' visual input through access to books and toys, and that caregivers may therefore direct infants' attention in a manner that supports their findings.

Evidence linking early attention to later self-regulatory outcomes, together with emerging intervention work, underscores the developmental relevance-and potential malleability-of early differences in visual attention.

In a large longitudinal sample of children from predominantly low-income, nonurban communities, poverty-related risk was negatively associated with infant sustained attention at 7 and 15 months, which in turn prospectively predicted pre-K executive function as well as teacher-rated effortful control and emotion regulation; infant sustained attention partially mediated associations between early poverty-related risk and each self-regulatory outcome (Brandes-Aitken et al., 2019).

text.text: Complementing these observational findings, intervention evidence suggests that core components of visual attention may be responsive to changes in infants' ecological conditions.

In a pilot study nested within a supplementary feeding trial in rural Sierra Leone, Leppänen et al. (2022) found that infants with moderate acute malnutrition showed a nonsignificant trend toward slower attention shifting at baseline (longer saccadic reaction times) relative to non-malnourished peers, but showed significant improvement relative to agematched controls after four weeks of supplementary feeding.

(2022)</ref> found that infants with moderate acute malnutrition showed a nonsignificant trend toward slower attention shifting at baseline (longer saccadic reaction times) relative to non-malnourished peers, but showed significant improvement relative to agematched controls after four weeks of supplementary feeding.

text.text: This suggests that early orienting dynamics can change over relatively short time scales when poverty-linked constraints such as undernutrition are addressed.
These findings motivate closer attention to the mechanisms through which socioeconomic context shapes early attentional organization.

Beyond material resources, social factors such as caregiver-infant interaction may influence fixation by scaffolding attention toward relevant targets during play and everyday routines, thereby supporting the development of endogenous attentional control.

In parallel, stress-related physiological processes associated with socioeconomic adversity may affect arousal regulation, producing differences in vigilance, distractibility, or persistence of fixation depending on contextual demands.
Importantly, these pathways are likely probabilistic rather than deterministic and may operate differently across attentional components and developmental periods (Blair and Raver, 2012).

text.text: The literatures reviewed above differ in what they can tell us about culture.

Cross-national studies come closest to examining culture directly, but they typically operationalize culture as country of residence and rarely measure the meanings, practices, or caregiving routines thought to produce attentional differences.

Research on multilingual, interracial, and socioeconomic experience often measure a specific experiential variable with some precision-such as the proportion of exposure to each language, the amount of interracial contact, or household chaos-and report graded associations with attention within a single society.

But they rarely ask whether these experiences carry different meanings in context, or are embedded in different practices, across cultural communities, and so they speak to effects of experience rather than effects of culture.
This division of labor leaves a gap.

On one side are studies showing that culture, broadly indexed, is associated with infant attention but that do not identify the experiences responsible; on the other are studies that identify experiences associated with attention but do not situate them culturally.

Closing the gap would involve examining the developmental niche directly-the settings of daily life, customs of care, and caregivers' beliefs and practices (Super & Harkness, 1986)-alongside attentional outcomes, within and across cultural communities, and testing whether the same proximal experience is associated with the same attentional component in different settings (Matsumoto & Yoo, 2006).

text.text: The synthesis below is organized by attentional components so that evidence from both kinds of studies can be compared at the level at which it is most informative.

We next synthesize the literature by decomposing infant visual attention into its component processes, allowing evidence from diverse sociocultural contexts to be evaluated according to the attentional operations it informs.

Across national contexts, variation in infant visual attention does not map cleanly onto simple contrasts such as WEIRD versus non-WEIRD, nor can it be explained by reified typologies such as analytic equals Western and holistic equals non-Western.
Instead, cross-national evidence may be most useful when interpreted at the level of attentional components.
Some findings implicate focal versus contextual processing; others implicate speed-accuracy trade-offs, orienting efficiency, or the informativeness of particular dependent variables.

Cross-national contrasts therefore identify candidate mechanisms, but they must be paired with more precise measures of proximal experience and with attention to methodological variability (see Figure 1 for a visual summary of findings).  1.

text.text: Crucially, these effects are often graded with experience and can emerge even when overall looking time does not differ, indicating that language exposure may modulate how attention is distributed rather than how much attention is deployed.
Findings on interracial face experience illustrate why the scope of an observed effect must be specified rather than assumed.

Greater experience with other-race faces may alter attention specifically within the face-processing system-for example, by changing how readily infants discriminate, scan, or maintain attention to faces from different racial groups.

Alternatively, such experience may shape broader attentional operations, such as the speed with which infants disengage from a stimulus, shift attention, or flexibly allocate attention across competing inputs.
Evidence from a face-based task alone cannot distinguish these possibilities.
Establishing a domain-general effect therefore requires showing that the same attentional pattern extends beyond faces to nonsocial or differently structured stimuli.

This distinction constrains claims appropriately while preserving the theoretical significance of the literature: sociocultural experience may tune face-specific perceptual processing, broader mechanisms of attentional control, or both, but the underlying nature of the effect must be determined through comparisons across tasks and stimulus domains.
SES-related findings further show that environmental influences on attention are not linear or uniformly directional.
Socioeconomic context appears to shape how infants regulate engagement and disengagement under varying levels of perceptual and informational load.

In some contexts, sustained fixation and demand-sensitive modulation align with higher SES; in others, broader sampling, faster updating, or reduced disengagement failure are associated with greater household unpredictability or chaos.

These patterns imply that attentional behaviors commonly treated as markers of maturity or efficiency may instead reflect calibration to local levels of environmental entropy, with functional consequences that depend on task demands and developmental timing.
The reviewed evidence is necessarily constrained by the small number of available studies, heterogeneity in designs, and uneven measurement of culture-relevant variables.

Apparent inconsistencies may reflect genuine differences in how attentional systems are calibrated across environments, but they may also arise from unmeasured cultural variables, stimulus familiarity, testing context, analytic choices, or mismatches between tasks and the attentional components they engage.
This is precisely why a culturally situated model must be component-specific, measurement-conscious, and cautious in its claims.
The model rests on four principles.
First, looking behavior should be interpreted at the level of attentional components rather than as a unitary measure.
Fixation duration, novelty preference, latency to shift, disengagement failure, gaze dispersion, pupil dilation, anticipatory looking, and gaze following do not index the same construct.
Second, demographic variables should be treated as important but imperfect proxies for proximal experience, rather than as explanations in themselves.

They provide essential information for situating samples and evaluating generalizability, but should be supplemented by more direct measures of culturally patterned experience-such as caregiving routines, social diversity, household organization, and environmental predictability-and integrated into the interpretation of attentional behavior.

Third, methodological features-including immediate task context, stimulus familiarity, perceptual salience, task structure, calibration quality, exclusion criteria, and analytic decisions-may interact with sociocultural experience and with individual differences such as temperament and arousal regulation.
Identifying these interactions depends on adequately capturing the relevant exogenous, contextual, and individual-level factors rather than treating them as background variation.

This requires a more situated approach in which a broader range of environmental and participant characteristics is measured and integrated into the interpretation of attentional behavior (see Singh, Barokova et al., 2024, for a framework to capture infants' demographic information).

text.text: Fourth and related, the functional value of an attentional pattern cannot be inferred from the behavior alone; it depends on the affordances and demands of the environments in which that pattern develops and is deployed.
This framework complements endogenous accounts of attentional development.
Models of alerting, orienting, and executive attention emphasize biologically constrained systems that mature over time and interact with experience (Posner & Rothbart, 2007).
text.formatted: Models of alerting, orienting, and executive attention emphasize biologically constrained systems that mature over time and interact with experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Posner & Rothbart, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: A culturally situated model extends this view by asking how culturally patterned input shapes the developmental calibration of those systems.

Endogenous capacities constrain what infants are able to attend to, but experience can shape what infants preferentially attend to, how readily they disengage, when novelty or familiarity is prioritized, and whether persistence or flexibility is more functional in a given ecology.
This framework also clarifies what it means to ask whether looking behavior is a reliable index of cognition.
Reliability and validity are not global properties of looking time; they are properties of particular measures used for particular inferential purposes.
A novelty preference may validly index discrimination or memory in a specific paradigm while also being moderated by infants' prior novelty orientation, language environment, or stimulus familiarity.
Similarly, slower disengagement may index immature control in one context but strategic persistence in another.
Rather than treating these possibilities as threats to looking-time methods, a culturally situated model treats them as testable hypotheses about construct validity.
The meaning of looking itself may also vary across cultural contexts.

Communities differ in how caregivers organize infants' attention-for example, in the relative emphasis placed on engagement with the caregiver versus engagement with objects and ongoing events (Bornstein et al., 1992; Chavajay & Rogoff, 1999)-and in infants' familiarity with screens, laboratory settings, and unfamiliar adults.

text.text: When researchers compare infants across cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic, or racialized contexts, it is important to ask whether the task engages the same attentional construct in each group and whether the dependent variable has the same meaning across contexts.
This does not require abandoning cross-group comparisons.

It requires designing them so that stimulus familiarity, task affordances, and analytic choices are not coarsely interpreted as cultural effects on the basis of difference or as evidence of universality on the basis of similar responses, and so that robust measures can be distinguished from measures that are expected to vary with experience.
A related concern is the valence attached to looking behavior.
Treating faster disengagement, longer looking, or greater focus on focal objects as a sign of developmental advancement assumes that the same pattern is adaptive everywhere.
Supporting that interpretation requires much broader sampling and an account of what a given looking pattern accomplishes in the real-world contexts where infants actually develop.
This does not require abandoning cross-group comparisons.
It requires designing them so that stimulus familiarity, task affordances, and analytic choices are considered relative to their functionality in context.
Large-scale collaborative efforts such as ManyBabies provide one powerful route toward this goal because they can harmonize protocols, diversify samples, and test moderation across laboratories.
However, culturally situated models cannot depend only on large consortia.

A single-laboratory study can also implement the framework by taking several concrete steps: specifying the attentional component targeted by the paradigm; measuring relevant proximal experiences and individual differences such as language variability, caregiver routines, household chaos, stimulus familiarity, social diversity, temperament, and arousal regulation, using available instruments such as household chaos scales (Matheny et al., 1995), detailed language-exposure measures (de Bruin, 2019), standardized demographic questionnaires (Singh, Barokova et al., 2024), and head-mounted cameras that capture infants' everyday visual input (e.g., Fausey et al., 2016); reporting demographic variables consistently; checking whether stimuli are similarly familiar and salient across participants; considering moderation by experience when sample size permits; and interpreting group differences relative to task demands rather than as default evidence of ability, deficit, or universality.

text.text: The framework also points beyond passive viewing in the laboratory.

Laboratory paradigms are valuable because they isolate specific attentional operations, but infants' everyday attention unfolds in multimodal, socially embedded contexts that include caregiver behavior, bodily activity, objects, routines, noise, and competing demands.

Naturalistic methods, including head-mounted eye tracking, home observation, video-based coding, and caregiver-report measures of routines and environments, can help determine whether laboratory patterns generalize to real-world attentional ecology.
Conversely, laboratory tasks can help identify which components of real-world attention are shaped by particular forms of experience.
In sum, moving toward culturally situated models of infant visual attention allows the field to retain the explanatory power of looking-based methods while strengthening their theoretical precision.
The central claim is not that infant attention is infinitely malleable, nor that culture explains all variation in looking behavior.

It is that attentional measures are produced by developing infants situated in structured environments, and that the field can make stronger inferences when endogenous mechanisms, proximal experience, task context, and measurement validity are modeled together.
